title: The river meets the sea
hookLine: the river god, proud of his flood, reaches the ocean and is humbled

lines: CAN'T TELL AN OX FROM A HORSE.
cards: It's the season of the autumn floods. Streams from everywhere pour into the Yellow River, and it swells so wide that, standing on one bank, you can't tell an ox from a horse on the other. The god of the river is thrilled.
He looks at all that water and decides that every beautiful thing in the world belongs to him. So he sets off downstream, heading east, riding his own current, to see where it goes.
That's how the Zhuangzi, a Taoist classic, opens its chapter called Autumn Floods.

teach.h: HE CAN'T SEE WHERE THE WATER ENDS.
teach.b: First, the arrival. The river god reaches the North Sea, turns to look east, and can't see where the water ends. All his pride goes out of his face.

He sighs to the spirit of the sea and admits it: there's an old saying about someone who has learned a little and thinks nobody can match him, and that, he says, was me. Second, the frog. The sea doesn't scold him.
You can't talk about the ocean to a frog in a well, the sea says: he's stuck in his small space.

teach.h: NOW I CAN TALK TO YOU.
teach.b: You can't talk about ice to a summer insect: he's stuck in his one season. The frog isn't foolish. His well is just all he's seen.

Third, the opening. Then the sea says the line the whole story turns on: now that you've come out beyond your banks and seen the great sea, you know how small you are, and so now I can talk to you about the great things.
The humbling isn't the end of the lesson. It's the door into it. Fourth, the sea's own size.
And here's the twist. The sea, which never fills and never runs dry, doesn't think of itself as big either.

teach.h: EVEN THE SEA IS A PEBBLE.
teach.b: Next to heaven and earth, it says, I'm like a pebble or a little tree on a great mountain.
Every size in this story is real, and every size is small next to a larger one. The river's flood was real. It just hadn't met the sea yet.

how: Readers of the Zhuangzi, a classic of Taoist thought, return to the Autumn Floods chapter for its picture of how every point of view is small beside a larger one.

o: a Chinese harvest festival held each October
a Taoist poem mourning a village lost to water
the Zhuangzi chapter where a river meets the sea

p: thinks all beauty belongs to him
can't be told about the ocean
calls itself a pebble on a mountain

s: the sea scolds the river god for his pride
it explains: the frog in the well, the summer insect. then it says now I can talk to you.
the sea thinks of itself as the greatest thing there is
next to heaven and earth, it says, it's like a pebble on a great mountain.
the humbling is the start of the river god's lesson
once he knows how small he is, the sea says it can talk to him about the great things.

games.q: you're the river god. you reach the sea and can't see where it ends. what do you do?
o: admit you thought too much of yourself.
games.why: he sighs and admits it: the old saying about the one who thinks nobody can match him was about him.

practice: Close your eyes and call up the biggest water you've ever stood beside: hear it, feel how far it went, and notice your own size next to it, without minding.
If a proud thought shows up, a win, a boast, a being-right, let it flow downstream to meet that water. If you pray, you can rest in that wideness.

wordCard.voice: Autumn Floods. The Zhuangzi chapter where the proud river god reaches the ocean, sees no end to it, and is humbled before he's ready to learn. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: autumn water, autumn floods, the title of chapter 17 of the Zhuangzi.
